newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Snow cover seen good for Russia winter grain crops.
newsitem.headline: Snow cover seen good for Russia winter grain crops.

text.p: Weather conditions in Russia are generally favourable for winter grain crops, although it is too early to predict the size of this year's grain harvest, industry sources said on Friday.

A covering of snow in the main producing regions bodes well for farmers, said Viktor Trenin, head of the State Meteorological Service, adding that early indications of winter-kill loss suggest it will be around average.
"At the moment the situation is very favourable for the winter crops, because there is a very good snow covering over the majority of growing regions," he said.
"Usually the statistical average (of winter-kill loss) is around eight to 10 percent. At the moment we think that this is what we will have," he said.
Trenin said that snow cover in the central growing regions of Volgo-Vyatsky and Povolzhsky was between 20 and 40 centimetres, and in a few cases 60 centimetres.
In the northern Caucasus region the snow covering is two to three times the "normal" level.
"On the one hand that helps to save the crops from frosts, and it's also very good for moisture levels when the snow melts," he said.
"In Western Siberia and the Urals, the areas under sowing are not that big, but the situation is also favourable there."
Industry sources said it was too early in the winter season to make accurate predictions about winter-kill levels.
"We may have a better idea some time in March," said a Russian grains analyst.

"There may yet be problems, because winter is not over," Trenin added. If temperatures rose sharply and then dropped again, for example, a layer of ice could form over the snow, damaging the crop when the snow melts, he explained.
Russia's net grain harvest in 1996 was officially 69.3 million tonnes, up from 1995 levels, but still one of the smallest harvests for thirty years.
Analysts have said that the outlook for the new crop is not particularly promising despite the helpful covering of snow, because of a reduction in the area sown to winter crops.
